meta.title: How the GB electricity market fits together
meta.subtitle: Four markets, one wire, and a settlement process that decides months later what actually happened.
meta.one_line: Electricity in Great Britain is bought and sold four times over — years ahead, days ahead, within the day, and after the fact — and the physical system is balanced by a fifth mechanism that only the system operator can call. A supplier is a participant in all of them at once, and its cost of serving a customer is not known on the day it serves them.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Everything on this page is a published feature of the GB energy market, readable by anyone — so it is readable by the simulated company too, the same way a real supplier reads the codes and the market reports. Nothing here is an internal of the simulation and nothing here tells the company anything its real counterpart could not look up.

claim_freshness.source: Elexon BSC settlement runs and glossary (II, SF, R1, R2, R3, RF, with RF at 14 months and the disputes run at 28 under the legacy timetable); MHHS Programme transition-to-new-settlement-timetable milestones (go-live 22 September 2025; RF 14 to seven months for settlement days from 1 October 2026, seven to four from 1 April 2027; migration to May 2027).

claim_freshness.found:
ONE MATERIAL SHARPENING AND ONE OVER-BROAD CLAIM; the page's substantive account of how a supplier buys, trues up and is settled is CORRECT and stands.

1. THE SETTLEMENT TIMETABLE WAS STATED IN THE PRESENT TENSE AND IT IS A DATED FACT. 'Re-run repeatedly over more than a year' is a true description of 2016-2025, the record this simulation is built on, and it is being falsified by MHHS on a published schedule whose first step lands three weeks after this check. A reader could not tell from the page which of the two it described. Now dated explicitly, with the run names the reader would need to look any of it up.

2. 'A supplier is not a participant here' was too strong about the Balancing Mechanism. True of a domestic supplier and of this simulation's company; not true as a rule, since a supplier with generation can hold a BM unit and virtual lead parties route domestic flexibility into the BM. Narrowed to the claim the evidence supports.

CONFIRMED UNCHANGED: gate closure at one hour ahead; the five market layers and their order; the forward/day-ahead/intraday structure; the three falsifiable shapes in 'what the data should look like'.
claim_freshness.note: Written 2026-08-24 to replace a stub. Six Knowledge pages shipped as identical empty templates and had been serving a heading with no content.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB electricity supplier does not buy electricity once. It contracts ahead for most of what it thinks its customers will use, trues that up as the delivery day approaches, and is then charged or paid for the difference between what it contracted for and what its customers actually took — a difference nobody knows precisely until settlement runs, months afterwards.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Think of it as promising to buy a quantity of something you cannot store, for people who have not yet decided how much of it they want.

A supplier looks at its book, forecasts how much its customers will use in each half-hour, and buys roughly that much in advance — mostly months or years ahead, because that is where the liquidity is and because buying at the last minute means taking whatever the price is. Closer to the day it adjusts, in the day-ahead auction and then intraday as the weather forecast firms up.

Then the day happens. Customers use what they use. Wind blows harder or less hard than forecast. The supplier's contracted volume and its customers' actual volume do not match, and the gap is settled at the imbalance price — a price the supplier does not choose and cannot see in advance.

The thing that surprises people is the timing. The supplier does not find out its real position on the day. Meter readings arrive late, estimates are used in the meantime, and settlement is re-run repeatedly as better data replaces worse. A supplier's accounts for last winter keep moving for a long time after last winter. Over the decade this simulation runs, the last scheduled re-run came 14 months after the day itself; that window is now being compressed by half-hourly settlement, and the rung below dates the change rather than leaving the reader to assume today's market works the way the record did.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
Five layers, and a supplier touches all of them.

**Forward and futures.** Standardised blocks — seasons, quarters, months — traded bilaterally or through brokers and exchanges. This is where a supplier fixes the bulk of its cost, and it is what makes a fixed-price retail tariff possible at all: you cannot sell a household a fixed price for a year unless you have already bought most of the energy.

**Day-ahead.** An auction that clears a price for every half-hour of tomorrow. This is the reference price most of the market marks against.

**Intraday.** Continuous trading up to close of the delivery period, where late forecast revisions get traded out.

**The Balancing Mechanism.** After gate closure — one hour before the half-hour concerned — only the system operator acts. It accepts bids and offers from generators and large flexible loads to keep supply and demand matched in real time. A DOMESTIC supplier is ordinarily not a participant here; it is a payer, through the balancing costs that flow back to it. That is a statement about this kind of supplier, not a rule: a supplier with generation of its own can hold a BM unit, and since the market opened to virtual lead parties an aggregator can bring domestic flexibility into the BM without being the supplier at all.

**Settlement.** Elexon determines, per half-hour and per supplier, what its customers actually consumed and what it had contracted, and charges or pays the difference. That determination is made repeatedly, because the meter data improves: an interim and initial run, then reconciliation runs R1, R2 and R3, then Final Reconciliation, with a disputes run later still.

**HOW LONG THAT TAKES IS A DATED FACT, NOT A PERMANENT ONE, AND THIS PAGE MEANS THE PERIOD THE SIMULATION RUNS.** Across 2016-2025 Final Reconciliation landed at 14 months after the settlement day and the disputes run at 28, which is where 'more than a year' on this page comes from. Market-wide Half-Hourly Settlement went live on 22 September 2025 and is compressing that timetable in steps: Final Reconciliation moves from 14 months to seven for settlement days from 1 October 2026, and from seven to four for settlement days from 1 April 2027, with initial settlement and R1 pulled in during 2027. Supplier migration runs to May 2027. So the long tail described here is a true account of the record this simulation is built on and an increasingly false account of the market as you read it.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
If that is how it works, three things follow and each is visible in published data.

**Prices should be far more volatile the closer you get to delivery.** A season-ahead contract moves slowly; a half-hour imbalance price can be an order of magnitude away from the day-ahead price for that same half-hour. The forward curve is not a forecast of the spot price so much as a price for certainty.

**A supplier's realised cost should differ from any single published price.** Its cost is a weighted blend across contracts struck at different times, plus an imbalance settlement it did not choose. Anyone quoting one wholesale number as 'the' cost of supply is quoting an input, not a cost.

**Last year's numbers should keep changing.** If settlement reruns are real, a supplier's reported volume for a past period moves as reconciliation runs land. A book that never restates is a book that is not settling.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
The simulation buys forward against a hedging mandate, settles half-hourly against real Elexon system prices, and carries the imbalance difference as a real cost. Its wholesale inputs are the published historical record for 2016–2025, not a generated series.

What it does NOT model is the Balancing Mechanism as a market the company can participate in. Balancing costs reach the company as costs; it never submits a bid. For a domestic supplier that is close to reality, and it is a real simplification rather than a hidden one.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
The relationship between forward prices and realised spot is not a solved question and nothing here claims it is. Whether hedging ahead is cheaper than buying spot over a long enough run is genuinely contested — the answer depends on the period you pick, and picking the period is where most confident answers come from.

This simulation takes a position on it only in the sense that its company follows a mandate and the results are then reported, including the years the mandate cost it money.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body:
No Balancing Mechanism participation. No Capacity Market auction behaviour (the charge is modelled, the auction is not). No interconnector trading strategy. No modelling of the supplier as a generator.

These are named rather than quietly absent because a reader who knows the market will look for them, and finding them missing without a note is worse than finding them missing with one.
